I'm working on a Debian derivative system, so this should also work in Ubuntu and such.

  1. Install QEMU. On Debian and derivatives the command is sudo apt-get install qemu.
  2. Download the Haiku image.
  3. Verify the checksum from the Haiku download page. On Debian and derivatives the command is sha256sum haiku-r1beta1-x86_64-anyboot.zip. Copy the hash from the terminal window and use the browser's Find in page command to find the hash on the downloads page.
  4. Make a directory for your virtual machine: mkdir -p ~/virtual-machines/haiku-r1beta1.
  5. Change to the new directory: cd ~/virtual-machines/haiku-r1beta1.
  6. Unzip the ISO image here: unzip ~/Downloads/haiku-r1beta1-x86_64-anyboot.zip
  7. Create a hard disk image to install Haiku onto: qemu-img create haiku-disk.img 2G
  8. Start the virtual machine to boot the Haiku ISO: qemu-system-x86_64 -m size=512M -cdrom ./haiku-release-anyboot.iso -drive file=./haiku-disk.img,index=0,media=disk,format=raw. Consult man qemu-system-x86_64 for details.
  9. The partition editor is not as nice as gparted, but it does seem to work. All these commands are available in the menu. Beware that Haiku doesn't use familiar keyboard shortcuts, so use the mouse! You need to create a disk label (aka partition table) before you can add a primary partition. I made a GPT disk label, and that worked for me.
  10. Format the new partition with the Be Filesystem.
  11. Mount the new partition.
  12. Quit the partition editor.
  13. Back in the installer menu, select the newly mounted partition as the target, and click the install button.

Enjoy!
